x: Your government One owner, several checks Groups of businesses that list the same officer, manager or registered agent in state corporate records and each gave to the same local candidate. Each group was checked by hand against the state's records before it was listed here. All elections All candidates Loading… Gifts over the $1,000 limit One organization, one candidate, one election Florida limits each contributor to $1,000 per election for a local candidate (s. 106.08, F.S.); the primary and the general each count as their own election. These are cases where a campaign's own reports show more than that from one organization, net of refunds. Each was checked by hand. Open means no explanation has been found yet. Resolved means it was explained (for example a reporting error, an amended report, a refund, a check meant for the general election, or an Elections Commission ruling), and the explanation is shown. Loading… About this list This is legal. Under Florida law each corporation or LLC is its own contributor with its own limit ($1,000 per election for local offices), so one owner's companies can each give. Giving in someone else's name is what the law forbids (s. 106.08(5), F.S.). A group here is a pattern in public records, not a finding of wrongdoing. How businesses are linked. Business contributors in the Supervisor of Elections reports are matched to the Florida Division of Corporations (Sunbiz) file. Businesses are grouped when they list the same person as an officer, manager or registered agent, matched by name and address. Corporate officers on 25 or more companies and registered-agent services are left out. Years. Groups are listed by the election the checks were for, newest first. Candidates often raise money a year or more ahead, so checks for a 2024 race can be dated 2023; each card says when its checks were written. Inactive businesses are flagged. A business marked Inactive is dissolved, revoked or no longer filing annual reports with the state; "since" is the last year it filed. Its gift was made while it was still filing. Over the limit. A reported overage is not a finding of wrongdoing. Reports can contain typing errors, a check written before the primary can be meant for the general election, and a campaign fixes an overage by refunding it. Only the Florida Elections Commission decides whether the law was broken. Data: /api/v1/datasets/over-limit-gifts . People aren't named. BayCounty.me doesn't name individual donors. Each business links to its public Sunbiz record. Something wrong? If a business is grouped by mistake, tell us and we'll correct it. The data is also at /api/v1/datasets/shared-owner-groups . x: Your government Bay County nonprofits Every local nonprofit, starting with the ones tied to public money and campaigns. Search for any one, or tap a card. Sources and method Which organizations. Every organization the IRS recognizes as tax-exempt with an address in Bay County (the IRS Exempt Organizations Business Master File), plus active Florida nonprofit corporations (Sunbiz) whose principal address is in the county. IRS and state records are joined by the EIN the corporation gives the state, then by exact name. Money. Revenue, expenses and assets come from the latest 990, 990-EZ or 990-PF the organization e-filed (2019 on). Small organizations file a 990-N postcard with no figures, and churches don't have to file. Government payment records are the site's contracts, check registers, tourism agency payments and CRA ledger, matched to the nonprofit by name. Grants are from Schedule I of local nonprofits' returns. Florida charity registrations. Charities that ask Floridians for donations must register each year with the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services. The registrations with a Bay County address come from its Check-A-Charity database: status, expiration, the revenue and the program, fundraising and management spending the charity reported, and its professional fundraising firms. Officers, directors and the tax ID (FEIN) come from the registration application each charity uploads; people the application marks as removed or exempt from public records are left out, and scanned applications without readable text are not read yet. Registrations are joined to the IRS and state records by FEIN, then by exact name; those that match neither are listed on their own. Churches and some small charities are exempt from registering, so a missing registration is not by itself a problem. Board members. 990 and 990-EZ returns list officers, directors, trustees and key employees with their hours and pay; 990-N postcards name a principal officer; the state lists up to six officers; Florida charity registration applications list officers and directors. Names are shown as filed and grouped across boards by last and first name (nicknames such as Bob and Robert count as one), so two people with a common name can be grouped together. "Shares board members" counts other local nonprofits whose latest filings list the same name. Businesses come from Florida corporate filings (Sunbiz officers and registered agents): "name and address" means the person on the nonprofit's own state filing is the same Sunbiz person; "name" means only one Sunbiz person in the county has that name. Campaign gifts are the business's own gifts in Supervisor of Elections reports. An "official" tag means the name was checked by hand against an elected official, department leader or candidate. Members pay dues to belong. A chamber is a nonprofit business league (501(c)(6)), not a government agency, and it isn't part of the U.S. or Florida Chamber. It connects, promotes and speaks up. Chambers run networking events, leadership classes and ribbon cuttings, keep a member directory, and take positions on local issues such as taxes, roads and the bases. Why it's on this site. Their boards bring together business owners, public agency heads and military leaders, some of their members do business with local governments, and the tourism agencies pay them for events and sponsorships. Serves: Callaway, Lynn Haven, Mexico Beach, Panama City, Panama City Beach, Parker, Springfield and unincorporated Bay County. Rip currents cause most lifeguard rescues on these beaches: if you're caught in one, swim parallel to shore, then back in. For a text when Panama City Beach's flags change, text PCBFLAGS to 888777. What the flags mean The international beach warning flags flown on every public beach here Double red: Water closed to the public Swimming and wading are against the law while double red flags fly (fines apply in Panama City Beach and unincorporated Bay County). Red: High hazard High surf and/or strong currents. Experienced swimmers only, and only close to shore. Yellow: Medium hazard Moderate surf and/or currents. Use caution. Green: Low hazard Calm conditions. Rip currents can still form near piers, jetties and sandbars. Purple: Dangerous marine life Jellyfish, stingrays or other marine life seen. Flies with another flag. Double red flags close the water: going in can bring a fine in Panama City Beach and unincorporated Bay County. No flag flying doesn't mean the water is safe. Flags recorded on 1 day since October 27, 2026: 1 yellow. Changing it (a rezoning or land use change) takes a public hearing before the planning board and a vote of the commission. Those votes are on How they voted and the agendas on Meetings . A site plan gets a development order. Bigger projects such as shopping centers, subdivisions and apartments file a site plan. Planning staff review it against the rules and issue a development order when it passes. Then come building permits. Each building needs a permit and inspections. The Census Bureau counts the new homes those permits allow every month, which is the yearly count below. State roads such as US 98, US 231, SR 77 and SR 390 belong to the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT). Its District 3 office in Chipley plans and hires the work, mostly with state fuel tax and federal money. The county and cities run the rest. Neighborhood streets and county roads are theirs. Much of that paving is paid for by the half-cent infrastructure sales tax voters approved in 2016. The plan comes first. Each year FDOT adopts a five-year work program: a study, then design, then buying land, then construction. A project's construction year can move as money changes. A new owner of an existing restaurant gets a new license, so a change of hands can show up here too. The state inspects, not the county. Inspectors from the Division of Hotels and Restaurants visit every licensed food business one or more times a year without notice, and again after a complaint. Violations come in three levels. High priority violations are the ones most likely to make someone sick, like food held at the wrong temperature. Intermediate and basic violations are things like missing thermometers or dirty floors. Serious problems get a follow-up, a fine or a closure. A warning means the inspector comes back to check. If it isn't fixed, the state can recommend a fine. Roaches, rodents, sewage or no hot water can close a place on the spot until it passes again. Where this comes from Inspections come from the public inspection files of the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation, Division of Hotels and Restaurants: every visit since January 2016. The current year's file is read every day. Licenses come from the state's daily list of licensed food businesses. A business inspected since 2016 that isn't on today's list is shown as no longer licensed. Food trucks, caterers and event vendors show only their city, since their license address can be a home. Results in plain words: the state's disposition codes are rewritten, for example "Call Back - Complied" becomes "Follow-up visit: fixed". The original code is in the data. License holders link to a profile when the name matches a company local governments paid or exactly one state corporate filing. A person is named only when they run a registered business at the license address. A franchise is usually licensed to its operator, not the brand. The two bases Tyndall Air Force Base Air Force · 325th Fighter Wing (Air Combat Command) Home of the 325th Fighter Wing, which is becoming an operational F-35A Lightning II wing (the first F-35As arrived August 1, 2023). x: Your government Officials' businesses The registered businesses and nonprofits that list a Bay County official, department leader or candidate as an officer, manager or registered agent, and where those businesses meet campaigns and public money. Each match was checked by hand against state corporate records. Everyone Only people with links Loading… About this list Where it comes from. The Florida Division of Corporations (Sunbiz) quarterly file lists each company's officers, managers and registered agent. Officials are matched by name, then each match is checked by hand (address, middle initial, the business itself) before it is listed. The bars. Each bar runs from the year the business was filed to today, or to its last filing (usually the dissolution) if it has closed. Sunbiz shows only current officers, so a bar says when the business existed, not exactly when the official joined it. From late 2026 on, BayCounty.me records when each officer first and last appears. Links. Two officials on the same business; an official's business giving to a campaign; a business that gave to a candidate and shares an officer with that candidate's own business (the shared person is counted, not named); and an official's business paid by a local government. A link is a fact in public records, not a finding of wrongdoing. Many are civic nonprofits that officials serve on as part of the job. Only officials and candidates are named. Other people on these businesses are never listed. Something wrong? Tell us and we'll correct it. The data is also at /api/v1/datasets/official-businesses and /api/v1/datasets/official-business-links . s: Bay County public projects followed from first budget to close-out: approvals, contracts, change orders, votes, payments and final cost, with questions raised by published rules, missing records and each agency's reply.
x: Your money Accountability console Public projects followed from the first budget to the day they close: what was promised, what was approved, every change order and payment we can find, and what it cost in the end. Where the record raises a question, it's flagged by a published rule and sent to the agency for an answer. Government All governments Bay County Panama City Panama City Beach Lynn Haven Callaway Springfield Mexico Beach 93 projects tracked $384.2M in those projects 42 with a question 28 records still missing 0 agency replies How it works Four steps for every project One timeline. Budgets, approvals, contracts, change orders, votes and payments from the site's records are put in order for each project, each with its source. Promised vs. delivered. The first firm figure is compared with the latest, and the planned finish with the real one. Flags follow rules. A flag is raised only by one of the published rules below, the same way for every government. A flag is a question, not an accusation. Agencies get to answer. Flags are sent to the agency, and its reply is posted beside them. Records we're missing become ready-to-send requests . Projects Year All years All governments Bay County Callaway Lynn Haven Mexico Beach Panama City Panama City Beach Springfield Any flag or none Any flag Cost grew more than 10% Running late Figures don't agree Who was paid isn't public yet Local share unclear Budgeted, but spending not shown Approval not found in the minutes More than one incentive, same place Dropped from the schedule All projects Reviewed project histories Contracts with change orders Sales tax projects Most questions first Biggest first Latest activity first Most cost growth Download CSV Loading projects… Show more The flag rules Every flag on this page comes from one of these rules. Each project's flags link back here. If a rule is unfair or applied wrong, tell us . Cost grew more than 10% When it's raised The latest firm figure (final cost, current contract total or current project estimate) is more than 10% above the first firm figure (the award or first budget). Over 25% is marked high. What it means The project costs noticeably more than the public was first told. Bay County and Panama City require board approval once change orders pass 10%. What it doesn't mean It does not mean money was wasted. Scope added on purpose, design and land costs, and price changes all raise totals. The flag asks the agency to explain the difference. Running late When it's raised A source reports the project finished more than 90 days after its schedule, or a sales tax project is not complete after the last year it was programmed for. Over a year is marked high. What it means The public waited longer than planned, which often costs money too. What it doesn't mean Delays are often caused by utilities, permits, storms or grant timing outside the agency's control. Figures don't agree When it's raised Two or more public documents give different amounts for the same project and period. What it means Residents cannot tell from the public record what the project costs or what was spent. What it doesn't mean The documents may count different things (one phase, the CRA share, the whole project). The agency can settle it with one breakdown. Who was paid isn't public yet When it's raised Money was spent or committed, but no record we have names the contractor or seller, or states the price. What it means The public cannot check who received the money or for how much. What it doesn't mean The information usually exists in the agency's files; it just wasn't in the report we read. A records request will usually get it. Local share unclear When it's raised The project mixes CRA or city money with state or federal grants, and no record says how much is local tax money. What it means The totals shown overstate what local taxpayers paid, by an unknown amount. What it doesn't mean Grants are good for local taxpayers. The flag is only about knowing the split. Budgeted, but spending not shown When it's raised A budget was set, but actual spending is under half of it for a year that has ended, or no record of actual spending was found. What it means The money may be sitting unspent, may have been moved, or the work stalled. What it doesn't mean Unspent budgets often roll over to the next year, and a delayed project may still be on track overall. Approval not found in the minutes When it's raised A change order appeared on an agenda, but the meeting minutes we read do not record a vote approving it. What it means We could not confirm the board approved the added cost. What it doesn't mean It may have been approved on a consent agenda, in minutes we have not read, or by staff within their authority. More than one incentive, same place When it's raised One address or company receives more than one grant or rebate from the same agency. What it means The total public support is easy to miss when each award is reported on its own. What it doesn't mean Programs usually allow this. The flag adds it up; it does not say it was wrong. Dropped from the schedule When it's raised A project was struck from the sales tax project schedule. What it means Money promised to voters for this project went elsewhere or is on hold. What it doesn't mean Schedules are amended when costs, grants or priorities change; the replacement project may be listed. Records still missing The questions above can usually be answered from records the agency already keeps. Each one opens a Florida public records request, written and ready to send. Right of reply, and how this was built Before a project's flags are treated as final, the agency is sent the flags and the records behind them, and asked to correct or explain. Its answer is posted with the project, in full or linked. Each project shows where that stands. Reviewed project histories were put together by hand from the CRA ledger, city capital schedules, resolutions and news reports. Contract timelines come from the contracts and change orders on the Contracts page, and votes from How They Voted . Sales tax projects come from the county's project schedule and map. News reports are marked as news. When an event's figure comes from a note on a source record rather than the document itself, it says so. Dollar totals add each project's latest figure once. Grants are included, so totals are more than local tax money alone. Download everything as JSON . Corrections: send one .

x: Glossary Plain-English guide Government money comes with a lot of jargon. Here is every term on this site, explained simply first, with more detail after. Anywhere on the site, a word with a dotted underline can be tapped for its short explanation. Community Redevelopment Agencies Property taxes and your bill Budgets and where money comes from How we label spending on this site Contracts, land and borrowing Public records Community Redevelopment Agencies Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) A savings jar for one neighborhood that needs fixing up. When the neighborhood's property gets more valuable, the extra tax money goes into the jar, and it can only be spent in that neighborhood. Florida law lets a city or county create a CRA for an area it officially finds run-down. The city commission usually acts as the CRA's board. It follows a written redevelopment plan and has an end date. Example: Lynn Haven's CRA covers about 695 acres around Ohio and Florida Avenues. CRA district The line drawn on the map around the neighborhood a CRA covers. Money raised inside the line is spent inside the line. Some CRAs have several districts. Panama City has four: Downtown, Downtown North, St. Andrews and Millville. Tax increment (TIF) The extra property tax a neighborhood brings in because its property became worth more after the CRA started. That extra is what fills the CRA's jar. On the day a CRA starts, the total property value inside it is written down. Every year after, the city and the county each pay into the CRA's trust fund the taxes on any value above that starting number. TIF stands for tax increment financing. Example: If a district was worth $100 million when it started and is worth $150 million now, the taxes on the $50 million difference go to the CRA. Base year The starting snapshot of how much all the property in a CRA was worth. Only growth above this number pays into the CRA. The base year is set when the CRA is created and stays the same for the life of the CRA. CRA trust fund The CRA's own bank account. Tax increment goes in, and by law it can only be spent on that CRA's plan. State law (Chapter 163, Part III) requires each CRA to keep its money in a separate trust fund and report how it was spent every year. Sunset date The day a CRA is scheduled to end. After that, the extra tax money goes back to the city and county budgets. A city can vote to extend a CRA's life. Lynn Haven extended its CRA to 2043 in January 2026. TIF rebate A deal where the CRA gives a builder back part of the new taxes their project creates, for a set number of years, to help get the project built. The rebate is paid only after the owner pays the full tax bill, and it has a maximum amount. Example: Panama City approved five TIF rebate awards downtown in December 2024. Façade or storefront grant Money a CRA gives a business owner to fix up the front of their building, usually matching what the owner spends. Most programs are 50/50: the CRA pays half, up to a limit, after the work is done. Property taxes and your bill Property tax (ad valorem tax) A tax based on what your house or land is worth. More valuable property pays more. Ad valorem is Latin for 'according to value.' Several governments each charge their own property tax, and all of them show up on one bill from the Tax Collector. Taxing authority Any government allowed to put a property tax on your bill, like the county, the school board or your city. Each one sets its own rate every year at a public hearing. Millage (mills) How property tax rates are written. One mill means $1 of tax for every $1,000 your property is taxed on. A rate of 5.5 mills is the same as 0.55%. Your bill adds up the mills from every taxing authority that covers your address. Example: 5 mills on a home taxed at $200,000 is $1,000 a year. Just value The Property Appraiser's estimate of what your property would sell for. It is set as of January 1 each year. Assessed value Your property's value after any limits on how fast it can go up. For a homestead, it usually rises more slowly than the market. Florida's Save Our Homes rule keeps a homestead's assessed value from rising more than 3% a year, or the rate of inflation if lower. Taxable value The number your tax is actually figured on: the assessed value minus any exemptions. It can be different for school taxes and other taxes, because one homestead exemption does not apply to school taxes. Homestead exemption A discount on property taxes for the home you live in full time, as long as you apply for it. The first $25,000 of value is exempt from all property taxes. A second amount, on assessed value above $50,000, is exempt from every tax except school taxes. It was $25,000 until 2024 and now rises with inflation: $25,722 in 2025 and $26,411 in 2026. Example: In 2025, a homestead assessed at $200,000 was taxed on $149,278 by the city and county and on $175,000 by the school board. Rolled-back rate The tax rate that would bring in the same money as last year from the same properties. If a government picks a higher rate, the law calls it a tax increase, even if the rate didn't change. New construction is left out of the calculation, so growth alone does not count as an increase. TRIM notice The postcard you get each August showing your proposed taxes and when the public hearings are. TRIM stands for Truth in Millage, Florida's law that sets the steps governments must follow before raising property taxes. Non-ad valorem assessment A flat fee on your tax bill for a service, like garbage pickup or fire protection. It isn't based on what your property is worth. It appears on the same bill as property taxes but is calculated per home, per acre or per unit instead of by value. MSTU An extra county tax area that pays for services in only part of the county, usually the areas outside cities. MSTU stands for Municipal Service Taxing Unit. Required Local Effort The school tax rate the state tells every school district to charge so it can get its share of state school money. The Legislature sets it each year. School boards can add a small discretionary rate and a capital rate for buildings. Save Our Homes cap A limit on how fast a homestead's taxed value can go up: 3% a year, or less if inflation is lower. Rentals, businesses and second homes have a looser 10% limit. The limits apply to assessed value, not to tax rates. Amendment 3 would lower the 10% limit to 5% for non-school taxes. Levy The total property tax a government collects in a year: its rate times all the taxable value in its area. Budgets and where money comes from Revenue Estimating Conference The state's team of economists that estimates how much money a new law or amendment would add or take away. Staff from the Legislature, the Governor's office and the Office of Economic and Demographic Research agree on one official estimate. Example: For Amendment 3, it estimated the loss for every county, city and special district. Fiscal year (FY) A government's budget year. In Florida it runs from October 1 to September 30. It is named for the year it ends in. Example: FY2026 runs from October 1, 2025 to September 30, 2026. General fund A government's main checking account for everyday services like police, parks and running city hall. Most property tax goes here. Money for special purposes is kept in separate funds. Enterprise fund An account for a service you pay for directly, like water and sewer. The bills you pay cover the service. These run like a small business inside the government. Special revenue fund Money that by law can only be spent on one thing, like gas tax for roads or a CRA's trust fund. State shared revenue Money the state collects, mostly from sales tax, and sends back to cities and counties. The biggest piece is the half-cent sales tax program. Cities and counties also get revenue-sharing money based on population and other factors. Charges for services Money a government earns by charging for things it provides, like water bills, garbage pickup, permits and park fees. Intergovernmental revenue Money one government gets from another, like federal grants or state shared revenue. Constitutional officers The elected county officials named in Florida's constitution: the sheriff, property appraiser, tax collector, clerk of court and supervisor of elections. Each has its own budget, and the county pays for most of them. Audit / annual financial report A yearly check of a government's books by outside accountants, to make sure the numbers add up and the rules were followed. Florida governments must file their audits and financial reports with the state. This site uses those filings. How we label spending on this site Spent The record says the money was actually paid out. Committed A contract or award has been approved, but not all of the money has been paid yet. Budgeted Money set aside in a plan. It may or may not be spent. Proposed An idea or request that hasn't been approved. Left out of totals Shown on the site, but not added into the totals, so the same dollar is never counted twice. Examples: a change order that is already part of a project total, a possible duplicate, or money that isn't from the CRA. Contracts, land and borrowing Change order An approved change to a contract after it is signed, which often adds cost or time. Right-of-way The land a road sits on plus the strip alongside it for sidewalks, utilities and drainage. Widening a road often means buying more right-of-way. Eminent domain When a government buys private land for a public project even if the owner doesn't want to sell. A court decides the fair price. The court process is called condemnation. Bond A way for a government to borrow money now and pay it back with interest over many years, like a mortgage. The yearly payments are called debt service. Community Development District (CDD) A special government created for one development to build and pay for its roads, pipes and other basics. The property owners there pay for it. Interlocal agreement A contract between two governments, like a city and the county. Public records Public records request Asking a government to show you or send you its records. In Florida, anyone can ask, and you don't have to say why. Florida's public records law is Chapter 119 of the Florida Statutes. Governments can charge for copies and for large amounts of staff time. Check register A government's list of every payment it made: who got paid, how much, when and for what. It is the most direct way to see where money went, and most cities don't post it online.

x: About & data Updates New pages, new data and corrections, newest first. Subscribe with any feed reader to get them as they happen: RSS feed . BayCounty.me launched on Oct 20, 2026. The first entries below are the initial pages going live. From here on, each new dataset, data refresh and correction gets its own dated entry. Change log Oct 27, 2026 This week in Bay County, by email. A new weekly email and page, This week in Bay County, puts the week in one place: events happening around the county, the public meetings on the calendar, and the votes, contracts and change orders that reached BayCounty.me in the past week, with split votes, failed motions, budgets and the biggest contracts first. Every company and official links to their profile. Sign up on the page for one short email on Monday mornings; every email has a one-click unsubscribe. /this-week · Email Alerts · /events · How They Voted · Contracts · Open Data Oct 27, 2026 What's happening in Bay County. The home page now opens its second section with what's happening today and coming soon around the county, and a new Events page lists the next two months in one calendar you can filter by town and kind: city and county events and meetings, library programs, visitor events in Panama City and Mexico Beach, and Panama City Beach Chamber events. Everything is read every morning from each organizer's public calendar, and each title links to the organizer's page. Chamber board and staff photos from the chambers' own websites now appear on the Chambers page. The apps have the same events on their home screens. Home · /events · /chambers · Meetings · Open Data · API Oct 27, 2026 Beaches and parks. Two new pages under a new Outdoors menu. Beaches shows today's beach flag and rip current risk (the flag color beach officials report to the National Weather Service, refreshed when you open the page), the next few days' surf forecast, what each flag means, the state health department's water quality samples at all 15 active sampling sites (each sample since late 2022, rated good, moderate or poor), and all 152 public beach accesses and the county's beach parking lots on a map, with wheelchair and drive-on access. Parks lists 107 public parks with their playgrounds, restrooms, fields, courts, piers and trails, 45 boat ramps and launches, 36 named trails, a map with directions, and each government's page for leagues, programs and rentals. The apps have the same screens. /beaches · /parks · Open Data · API Oct 27, 2026 Building, development and road projects. Two new pages. Building and development shows how many new homes are permitted each year since 2016 in the county and each city (from the Census Bureau's permit survey), and the commercial buildings, subdivisions and apartments in the county's planning review, with their status and dates on a map. Road projects shows the state highway work under way and what each FDOT contract costs, FDOT's five-year plan for local roads, the contractors (linked to their profiles, with what local governments paid them), and the county and city road jobs paid for by the half-cent sales tax. Both refresh every week, and the apps list the same records. /development · /roads · Sales Tax Projects · Open Data · API Oct 27, 2026 Public schools. A new Schools page covers every public school in Bay County, district and charter. Type an address to see its zoned elementary, middle and high school (from the school district's attendance zones); see the school calendar, from days off and early release to graduations and School Board meetings, refreshed daily; and open any school for its students, teachers, enrollment since 2016 and the nonprofit that runs it if it's a charter school. A chart shows district enrollment by year, including the drop after Hurricane Michael, and a list shows the schools that closed since 2016. State school grades and spending per school are being added from the Florida Department of Education. The address report links to the same schools, the API has a new endpoint for the schools zoned for any address, and the apps have the page too. /schools · My Address · /governments/bay-district-schools · Open Data · API Oct 27, 2026 Emergencies, alerts and hurricane prep. A new Emergencies and alerts page shows what is happening now in Bay County, checked every 5 minutes: National Weather Service watches and warnings, evacuation orders, open shelters, boil-water notices, road closures from FL511 and the cities, and storm updates from the county and city alert centers. Type an address to see its evacuation zone, whether an order covers it and the nearest shelters, and see every county shelter on a zone map. A Hurricane prep page covers a plan and a kit, sandbags, generator safety and what to do after a storm, every federal disaster declaration since 2016 and the FEMA housing aid and flood insurance money that reached each ZIP code after past storms (totals only). The apps can send notifications for warnings, evacuation orders, shelter openings, boil-water notices and agenda items near a saved place. /emergency · /hurricane-prep · Email Alerts · Open Data · API Oct 27, 2026 Military and the bases. A new page covers Tyndall Air Force Base and Naval Support Activity Panama City: what each base does, who commands it and the units on it, and the latest news stories from the 325th Fighter Wing, the 601st Air and Space Operations Center, NSA Panama City, the Navy's Panama City research lab and the Navy Experimental Diving Unit, read every day from their public feeds. It also lists every federal contract since 2016 to a company based in Bay County, from USAspending.gov: $3.9B to 239 companies, a little over half from the Defense Department and most of the rest from the Coast Guard. Each company links to its profile, where federal money now shows next to local government payments and campaign gifts. The apps have the same screen. /military · People · Open Data · API Oct 27, 2026 Chambers of commerce. A new page covers Bay County's two chambers of commerce, the Bay County Chamber and the Panama City Beach Chamber: who sits on their boards and staff (each name links to a profile with the person's other boards and records), the organizations those board members represent and what local governments paid them, upcoming chamber and community events, regular programs such as First Friday and Friday at the Beach, each chamber's IRS filings, and the tourism agency money paid to them. Board lists are copied from the chambers' own websites; no contact details are published. The apps have the same screen. /chambers · /connections/nonprofits · People · Open Data · API Oct 26, 2026 Where our data comes from. A new page lists every source behind BayCounty.me: each government's agenda system, calendar, minutes, budgets and fee schedules, and every state and federal database we use (Florida Auditor General, Department of Revenue, EDR, Sunbiz, the Supervisor of Elections, IRS filings, OpenFEMA and more). For each one it shows the link, whether we fetch it automatically or read it by hand, how often, what we take and how we check it, plus a count of every website our records cite. A notice at the top of every page also says the data is still being loaded and checked, so some totals may change. /data-sources · About · Open Data Oct 25, 2026 The site now starts in 2016. BayCounty.me now covers 2016 onward: fiscal year 2016 for budgets and other yearly figures, and 2016 for dated records. Older figures came off every page, download and the API: FY2015 budgets and audited actuals, CRA tax increment from FY2003 to FY2015, CRA spending records from before 2016, officeholder terms that ended before 2016, older events in the Accountability timelines (and the Front Beach Road Segment 1 project, built 2009 to 2013), and nonprofit board seats, grants and charity registrations from before 2016. Year pickers start at 2016. /public-money/budget-compare · Governments · /public-money/cra-tax-increment · CRA Spending · /public-money/accountability · /connections/nonprofits · People · Open Data · API Oct 25, 2026 Every local campaign since 2016. Campaign money now goes back to 2016. A new Past elections page lists every candidate who ran for a local office in Bay County from 2016 through 2025, winners and losers (342 campaigns that raised $5.2M), with what each raised and spent and every business, committee and party that gave. Those gifts also feed the Connections network, the vendor pages' donor matches and people's profiles, and each past candidate has a profile. Gifts from individual people are still counted only in totals. The Supervisor of Elections' online records start in 2016, so 2015 is not included. Past Elections · 2026 Elections · Connections · Campaign Gifts · People · /public-money/vendors · Open Data · API Oct 25, 2026 How much property tax goes to the CRAs. A new page estimates how much property tax Bay County and the cities pay to the seven Community Redevelopment Agencies each year: about $28.7M in FY2025, $25.8M of it from Bay County and three-quarters of it to Panama City Beach's Front Beach Road CRA. It shows who pays, what has been paid since FY2016, sunset dates and what could still be paid under three growth scenarios, checked against the county's own budget figures. The method and the missing years are on the page. /public-money/cra-tax-increment · Tax Dollars · Amendment 3 · Governments · Open Data · API Oct 25, 2026 Fewer pages, more on each government. Each government's page now carries its whole budget (every fund and department, and what each service costs per resident), every debt and bond, every audit finding from the last three years, and its savings ideas. Compare shows the side-by-side totals, including cost per resident by service. Tourism agency payments moved onto the Tourist tax page, county officers and officials' pay onto People, and the money map into Connections as Donors and votes. The old pages send you to the new spot. Governments · Compare · Tourist Tax · People · Connections · Tax Dollars Oct 25, 2026 Budgets back to 2016. The budget comparison now reaches back further. Bay County has every adopted budget from FY2016 to FY2027, fund by fund, from the county's budget archive. Panama City has FY2017 to FY2022 by fund group, read from its scanned budget books, and its General Fund for FY2016 and FY2023-24 using the city's audited financial reports, and Lynn Haven adds FY2020 with every fund and department. Audited revenue and spending for the county and all seven cities now go back to FY2016. For Panama City Beach, Callaway, Springfield, Parker, Mexico Beach and the school district, the General Fund budget for FY2021 to FY2025 comes from each year's audited financial report (Parker back to FY2016); their older budget books aren't posted online. The page lists which years each government has. /public-money/budget-compare · Governments · Open Data Oct 25, 2026 Compare a budget across years. A new page compares any government's budget in two fiscal years, such as Lynn Haven FY2025 and FY2026 or FY2022 and FY2026: the total, the General Fund, every department, every service and every fund, with the dollar and percent change. Lynn Haven has every adopted budget from FY2021 to FY2027 line by line, read from the city's budget documents; the other governments have FY2026 and, where posted, FY2027 lines, plus totals for earlier years. Audited revenue and spending can be compared for FY2021 to FY2024. Lynn Haven's FY2025 budget is now the original adopted figure ($52.2M); the city amended it to $64.9M at mid-year. /public-money/budget-compare · Compare · Governments · API · Open Data Oct 24, 2026 Business owners who gave are now named. People who run a registered business and gave to a local campaign are now listed by name, with the businesses they run and every campaign they gave to. A donor is listed only when the name and street address on the campaign filing are the same as an officer, manager or registered agent on the state business registry. Other individual donors are still counted only in totals, and addresses are never shown. Campaign Gifts · People Oct 24, 2026 Profiles for every name, linked everywhere. Every elected official, department leader and 2026 candidate now has a profile page with where they serve, campaign gifts from businesses and groups, recorded votes, votes on donors' contracts, pay and a map of their connections. Every other company, nonprofit, nonprofit board member, registered business and committee in the records has a profile too, with every documented connection and its source. Vendor and government pages gained the same connection map. Names of officials, companies and nonprofits are now links to their profiles across the site. Individual campaign donors are still never named, and officials' board seats and businesses appear only after an editor checks the match. People · Connections · /connections/nonprofits · /public-money/vendors · Governments · API · Open Data Oct 24, 2026 Connections: one network for every government. Campaign gifts and payee connections now have their own section, Connections, instead of sitting under the CRA pages. The network covers every government and agency with payment records: the county, the cities, the redevelopment agencies and the tourism agencies, across contracts, change orders, emergency purchases, check registers, tourism payments and the CRA ledger. It shows business gifts to every official who approves that spending, not only CRA board members, so 29 businesses that were paid and gave to a campaign now appear, up from 4. Campaign Money is now Campaign Gifts, and it and the Money map moved into the section; old links still work. Only businesses, PACs and committees are named as donors. Connections · Campaign Gifts · CRA Spending Oct 23, 2026 Savings finder: where governments could spend less. A new page lists places Bay County's local governments could spend less, found in records already on the site: Front Beach Road segments still ahead after the finished ones ran over, CRA capital budgets left mostly unspent, engineering bought in many separate task orders, and services such as plate readers and paving bought separately. Each opportunity shows the projects or ledger rows it rests on, a low and high estimate with its stated assumption, the next question to ask and a ready-to-send records request. Estimates are illustrative, not findings that money was wasted. Governments · /public-money/accountability · CRA Spending Oct 23, 2026 CRA network: payees, connections and campaign gifts. A new page shows every payee in the CRA ledger as a network: who each redevelopment agency paid, payees tied to each other by the same project, address or subcontract, and business campaign gifts to the officials who sit as each CRA's board. Four businesses both received money from a CRA record and gave to a campaign. A map and a ranked payee list use the same filters. Only businesses and PACs are shown as donors, and a gift and a payment together are facts about the records, not evidence of why either happened. Connections · CRA Spending Oct 23, 2026 Pages now open on the current year. Lists and tables with several years of records now open on the newest year that has records, never past the current fiscal year, with All years one tap away. That covers the Accountability console (and its headline numbers), CRA Spending, Contracts, How They Voted, Sales Tax Projects, the Hurricane Michael FEMA ledger, audit findings and other multi-year tables. A year with only a few stray records is skipped. Who Gets Paid now sorts by FY2026. Add ?year=all (or a year) to any page link to choose. Debt lists still show everything owed today. /public-money/accountability · CRA Spending · Contracts · How They Voted · Sales Tax Projects · Hurricane Michael · Governments · Tourist Tax Oct 23, 2026 Accountability console: projects from budget to close-out. A new page follows public projects from the first budget to the day they close: approvals, contracts, change orders, the votes on them, payments and the final cost, each with its source. Questions are raised only by nine published rules (cost growth over 10%, running late, figures that don't agree, an unnamed payee and others), the same way for every government, and each is a question for the agency rather than a finding. Each project shows the records that would answer its questions, as ready-to-send records requests, and where the agency's reply stands. It starts with 18 project histories reviewed by hand, 37 contracts with change orders and 39 scheduled sales tax projects. /public-money/accountability · Records Request · Open Data Oct 22, 2026 A privacy page, and data for the iPhone app. A new privacy page says what the site and the BayCounty.me iPhone app collect: no accounts, no ads and no tracking. The site now also publishes the files the app reads, in /data/app: the tax and Amendment 3 calculators, the glossary, company and people profiles and the money map. They hold the same information the pages already show. /privacy · API Oct 21, 2026 Company pages, and one map of public money. Every company with more than one record now has its own page: its contracts, change orders, payments, CRA money, gifts from the business to campaigns, and the votes that approved its contracts with how each member voted. A gift near a vote does not show why anyone voted the way they did. A new map shows CRA spending and 1,062 sales tax projects over CRA districts and city limits. Hurricane Michael projects are not on it because FEMA does not publish their locations. /public-money/vendors · Sales Tax Projects · Contracts · Tourist Tax · Connections Oct 21, 2026 New votes, FY2027 budgets, contracts and tourism payments. Added 30 votes (Panama City CRA and Commission, Callaway Commission and CRA) with each member's vote; the FY2027 budgets adopted in September for all nine governments; 17 contracts, mostly Springfield and Callaway; and tourism agency payments for 18 more months, each checked against the register's printed totals. Bay County Commission minutes after June 16 are not posted yet. How They Voted · Tax Dollars · Contracts · Tourist Tax · CRA Spending Oct 21, 2026 My Address: your officials, nearby spending, and privacy. My Address now links each local official to how they voted and to campaign money, lists CRA spending and sales tax projects near you, and links to your government's contracts, meetings and budget. To protect owners' privacy it no longer shows which kinds of exemptions a parcel gets (such as disability or veteran exemptions); it shows homestead and one total for all other exemptions. My Address · Exemptions Oct 21, 2026 Share any view; alerts you choose; Spanish pages. Filters now stay in the page link, so you can share exactly what you are looking at. Search results open the record itself. You can now get an email when a contract over an amount you pick is approved, when a board member votes, or when an agenda mentions a word you choose, and change what you follow at any time. Tax Dollars, Fees and Bills, Exemptions, Elections and Meetings are now in Spanish. Email Alerts · Search · What's new Oct 21, 2026 Contracts: how much each contract grew. Change orders are now added up for each contract and measured against its original amount, instead of listed one by one. Of the 22 contracts whose original amount is known, 12 grew by more than 10%, the point where Bay County and Panama City rules require board approval for the added cost. Each bar opens to its change orders, reasons and sources. Contracts whose original amount wasn't in the agendas are listed separately, and where an agenda states the new contract total, that total is used. Every individual change order is still listed below. Contracts Oct 21, 2026 Contracts: one name per company, and company cards. Agendas, check registers and campaign reports spell the same company many ways, so the contract winners list was splitting some firms into two or more entries. The 322 contracts used 206 spellings; they now resolve to the companies behind them. Marshall Brothers , for example, had been listed at $11.1M and is now ranked sixth at $24.0M. A new Look up a company section shows everything on the site for one company: contracts by government next to what each government paid it (where a check register shows it), change orders, emergency purchases, campaign gifts from the company, and votes on its contracts by officials it gave to. Insurance pools owned by governments ( Florida League of Cities , PGIT) are no longer counted as contractor wins. Contracts Oct 21, 2026 Money map: full roll calls on donor contract votes. The table of votes on a donor's contract now shows each vote once, with every board member's vote, not only the members who received a gift from the business. Members who got a gift are listed first, with the amount and date. Most of these contracts passed unanimously on the consent agenda. One vote that had been left out was added: Panama City's June 24, 2025 award of the Millville plant generator bid to Marshall Brothers , which the minutes record under an unrelated plat item. Connections Oct 21, 2026 Sort, filter and download every list. Every table and list on the site can now be sorted by clicking a column heading, filtered with a search box (and drop-downs where a column has a few values), and downloaded as a CSV of exactly the rows on screen, in the order shown. Lists open newest first, then A to Z; upcoming meetings open soonest first. What's new Oct 21, 2026 An API for BayCounty.me. Every dataset on the site is now available through a free, read-only API with filtering, sorting and CSV output, plus an MCP server so AI assistants can look up and cite these records directly. API Oct 21, 2026 Correction: Money map. The first version of the Money map overstated connections. It counted a donor's contracts again for every official the donor gave to, which roughly doubled the government totals, and it drew lines from officials to governments they don't serve on. The map now puts each donor in the middle: campaign gifts on one side, the governments that pay the donor on the other, each counted once. It marks only gifts to an official whose own government pays that donor, and lists the recorded votes those officials cast on that donor's contracts. The heat map that credited contract dollars to individual officials was removed. Connections Oct 21, 2026 Who's running in 2026. Every local race on Bay County ballots this year, with each candidate's platform in their own words, links to their campaigns, and their campaign money: what they raised and spent, how much came from individuals, organizations and their own pockets, and every business or committee that gave. Races already decided are shown separately. 2026 Elections Oct 21, 2026 Property tax exemptions, and exemptions on My Address. A new page shows every property tax exemption in the 2026 tax roll, from homestead to disabled veterans, with how many homes get each and how much tax it takes off bills. My Address now lists each exemption on a home by name and uses the certified school and non-school taxable values, which corrects estimates for fully exempt homes and for seniors with the county senior exemption. Exemptions · My Address Oct 21, 2026 School Board votes, and more city votes. How They Voted now includes 104 School Board votes from January 2024 to September 2026 with each member's vote, including budgets, millage and major contracts; all 2024 Panama City Beach council votes, including the FY2025 budget; and Springfield votes from mid-2024 to October 2026, including both final budget hearings. How They Voted Oct 21, 2026 Money map. An interactive map of which businesses and groups gave to which officials, and where those same donors hold contracts with a local government, plus heat maps of giving by government and of contract dollars held by each official's donors. Connections Oct 21, 2026 Budget explorer. Open any government's FY2026 budget: spending by fund, General Fund spending by department, and revenue by source. Includes Callaway's and Parker's adopted budgets, which weren't on the site before. Compare Oct 21, 2026 Who gets paid: tourism agencies. Payments by Visit Panama City Beach, Destination Panama City and the Mexico Beach CDC, read from the Clerk of Court's check registers and checked against each month's printed total. Tourist Tax Oct 21, 2026 Every bond, note and loan. The Debt page now lists each of 61 bond, note and loan issues with the amount borrowed, what is still owed, the rate, the final payment date and what it paid for. Compare Oct 21, 2026 A page for each government. Bay County, the School Board and each of the seven cities now have one page that pulls together who runs it, its budget and property tax rate, debt, audit findings, recorded votes, contracts, projects and upcoming meetings. Governments Oct 21, 2026 Compare governments side by side. Pick any governments and compare budgets, tax rates, debt and staffing, in total or per resident. Compare Oct 21, 2026 Upcoming public meetings. Every board's next meetings, with agenda links and the money items on each agenda, checked daily. Add them all to your phone or computer calendar with one link. Meetings Oct 21, 2026 Campaign money and contracts. The most recent campaign of each current elected official: how much they raised, from individuals and organizations, and which donors also hold contracts with local governments. Individual donors are counted, not named; each official's full report is linked. Campaign Gifts Oct 21, 2026 Request a public record. Pick a government and a record this site is missing, or describe your own, and get a ready-to-send Florida public records request with the right office's contact details. Records Request Oct 21, 2026 Open data downloads. Every dataset on the site, as CSV and JSON files you can open in a spreadsheet, with a description of each column. Open Data Oct 21, 2026 Zoning and development near your address. My Address now shows the zoning and future land use at the address, development projects and orders within half a mile, recent rezonings, and conditional uses nearby. My Address Oct 21, 2026 BayCounty.me en español. My Address, the records request tool and the glossary are now available in Spanish. Mi dirección, solicitudes de registros y el glosario, en español. En español Oct 21, 2026 Address lookup understands more ways of typing an address. My Address now finds addresses typed with full street types (Drive, Avenue, Boulevard), directions (North, West), highway forms (Hwy 98, US 98, County Road 2321), Saint or St., spelled-out numbers (Tenth Street), MLK, unit numbers, and a city, state and ZIP on the end. If a street type is wrong, it shows the closest matches. My Address Oct 21, 2026 Votes: filters and corrections. Filter recorded votes by government, member, year and outcome, sort by date, amount or closest margin, and share a filtered view by link. Corrections checked against the original minutes: removed two Lynn Haven votes counted twice from a second copy of the same minutes; fixed member votes on a Lynn Haven CRA vote and a Panama City Beach vote that had been misread; restored amounts cut off or misread from scanned pages; and noted fiscal-year and resolution-number typos that appear in the minutes themselves. How They Voted Oct 21, 2026 Clearer vote summaries. Every recorded vote now has a plain-English headline and summary saying what was decided, rewritten from the motion in the minutes. The earlier text was pasted from the minutes and was often hard to read. Each card shows who voted which way and links to the minutes. How They Voted Oct 21, 2026 Correction: flood zones on My Address. Flood zones now come live from FEMA's National Flood Hazard Layer, which reflects Bay County's October 24, 2024 flood maps. The earlier lookup used an older county copy that missed high-risk zones for some addresses (about 8% in a sample of 300) and showed outdated base flood elevations. Results now also show the FIRM panel and any map revision, with a link to check the address on FEMA's map. Thanks to the readers who reported it. My Address Oct 21, 2026 Link previews. Every page now shows a title, summary and image with its headline number when a link is shared in a text, email or social post. Home Oct 21, 2026 Send a correction from the site. A contact form on the About page sends corrections, records and questions straight to the BayCounty.me team. Email is optional and only used to reply. About Oct 21, 2026 Correction: Lynn Haven commission, and a cleaner officials page. Corey Langford is listed as Lynn Haven's fifth commissioner; Judy Tinder's recorded votes remain on the votes page as a former member. The officials page now shows each board as a simple roster, with notes under names and county officers as cards. Springfield and Parker are described as clerk-run cities with no manager, and Parker's City Clerk, Rachelle Stanley , is listed. People · How They Voted Oct 20, 2026 How they voted. Recorded votes on budgets, tax rates, contracts, land and borrowing, with every member's vote and split votes first. Now covers the County Commission and every city: 351 votes, 115 of them split. How They Voted Oct 20, 2026 Contracts and vendors. Major contracts approved by Bay County and its cities since October 2022: winners, how they were awarded, change orders, emergency purchases, the bidding rules, and who the county actually paid the most. Contracts Oct 20, 2026 Fees, utility bills and who runs Bay County. Every flat fee on Bay County tax bills, a typical monthly water, sewer and garbage bill in each city, and a guide to every elected seat, appointed manager and top salary. My Address now shows the actual fees on each parcel. Fees & Bills · People · My Address Oct 20, 2026 Designed PDF reports, and a new home page. Export PDF

s: What BayCounty.me is, where its information comes from, and how to send a correction.
x: About About BayCounty.me BayCounty.me is an independent, free website and app that puts Bay County, Florida public records in one place, in plain language. It covers all nine local governments: Bay County, Bay District Schools, Panama City, Panama City Beach, Lynn Haven, Callaway, Springfield, Parker and Mexico Beach. What you can find here Living here . Look up any address for its tax bill, schools, trash day, officials and nearby projects. Restaurant inspections, new businesses, road and building projects, beaches, parks, events, government jobs, emergency alerts and hurricane prep. Your money . Budgets by year, tax rates and fees, contracts and vendors, CRA and sales tax spending, Hurricane Michael recovery, and an accountability console that follows major projects from approval to final cost. Your government . Every elected official and department leader, their pay, how they voted , campaign gifts , and the business and nonprofit ties between people, companies and governments. Elections . Your ballot, where and when to vote, and results since 2016. Get involved . Meetings with their agendas and minutes, public notices, records requests, email alerts, and an Ask page that answers questions from the records on the site. Everything is also free to download as open data or use through the public API . Where the information comes from Every figure comes from a public record: budgets, audits, annual financial reports, meeting agendas and minutes, resolutions, campaign finance reports, state business filings, GIS map layers and state inspection data. Each one links to its source, and records go back to 2016. An automated reader helps pull votes and agenda items out of long meeting documents, and those are checked against the source before they count. See every source we use , with links and how we process each one. BayCounty.me is not run by, and does not speak for, any government. What the labels mean Spent : the record reports the money as paid. Committed : a contract or award has been approved but is not fully paid. Budgeted or Proposed : a plan or appropriation, not a payment. Totals count each dollar once. When one record is part of another (a change order inside a project total, for example), it stays visible but is left out of the totals. Who runs it BayCounty.me is built and run by Flux Labs , a managed IT company in Panama City. We live and work here, and we built this because public records should be easy to read without filing a request or digging through a PDF. The site has no ads and doesn't track you, and it isn't paid for by any government, candidate or campaign. Corrections, records and questions Found an error, or have a public record that fills a gap? Send it here. Corrections are dated on the page they affect and listed under What's new . What's this about? What BayCounty.me and its iPhone and Android apps collect: no ads, no tracking, and optional accounts for your home and for the realtor console.
x: Privacy BayCounty.me doesn't sell, share or track you. There are no ads and no tracking cookies, on the website or in the iPhone and Android apps, and nothing we count can pick you out. Accounts are optional: residents can sign in to save their home, and agents to use the realtor console. The website Visits. The site counts page views with Vercel Web Analytics, which uses no cookies and doesn't identify you. Email alerts. If you sign up, we keep your email address and what you chose to follow, so we can send the emails. Every email has a link to change or stop them. To have your address deleted entirely, email us. Contact form. Your message, name and email come to us by email so we can answer. They aren't added to any list. API. Requests to the public API are logged with the caller's IP address for 90 days to stop abuse, then deleted. Ask. Questions you type on the Ask page are sent to an AI service to write the answer, along with the public records it looks up. BayCounty.me doesn't save your questions or the answers; it logs only how many were asked (with a scrambled form of your IP address, to enforce limits) and what they cost. Please don't type personal information. Your account (My home). If you sign in at My home or in the app, we keep your email address, the first name you give (if any), the home address you save and what you asked to hear about, so we can show and send you what's happening near your home. Sign-in uses a code sent to your email; there are no passwords. A sign-in cookie keeps you signed in on the website. Your home address is never shown to anyone else, never published and never in a log; the feed uses it only to find what's nearby. You can change it, stop the emails, or delete your account and everything in it from My home at any time. Realtor console. Agents who sign in to the realtor console have an account under their email address. We keep the branding they save (name, brokerage, contact details, logo, photo and colors) and the addresses they've run reports for, so they can run them again. A sign-in cookie keeps them signed in for 30 days. None of it is shared or shown to anyone else, and an agent can delete the account, branding and history from the console at any time. Addresses sent to the address report are not logged. My Address. Address lookups go straight from your browser to Bay County's and FEMA's public map servers. BayCounty.me doesn't receive or store what you look up. The iPhone and Android apps No ads or tracking. The app has no advertising and no tracking. Signing in is optional; without an account it sends nothing about you to BayCounty.me. Anonymous usage counts. Once a day, when you open the app, it sends how many times it was opened and which screens were viewed since the day before, with the app version and whether it's an iPhone or Android. Nothing that identifies you or your phone is sent: no name, account, address, device id or location, and the IP address isn't stored. We see only totals, such as how many phones used the app today and which screens are used most. You can turn this off in the app under About, Share anonymous usage counts. BayCounty.me pages you open from the app are marked as coming from the app in the website's visit counts. If you sign in. Signing in to My home in the app uses the same account as the website: your email address, your saved home address and your choices are kept as described above, so the app, the website and your emails agree. Signing out removes the account from the phone; deleting the account deletes it everywhere. Your address and location. If you save a home address without signing in, it stays on your phone. If you tap "Use my location," the app asks permission first and uses your location once to find your address on Bay County's public map server. It isn't stored or sent anywhere else. Downloaded data. The app saves copies of the public records it shows so it works offline. Deleting the app deletes them. Maps. The Android app draws its maps with OpenStreetMap tiles, so OpenStreetMap's servers see your IP address when they send them, as any website would. The iPhone app uses Apple Maps. Crash reports. If you've allowed it in your phone's settings, Apple or Google may share anonymous crash reports with the developer. Questions Email hello@fluxlabs.net or use the contact form . BayCounty.me is run by Flux Labs in Panama City, Florida.

A dashed line is a documented link between two payees: the same project, the same address, or one working as the other's subconsultant. Each one cites its record. A red line is a business campaign gift , and a dotted line joins an official to the board they sit on. A city commission also sits as its redevelopment agency's board. CRA ledger items that are only proposed or planned stay on the CRA ledger . Payees are matched to the site's vendor list by name. 598 payees are named; grant programs whose recipients aren't named are grouped, and private home addresses are left out. Campaign gifts come from officials' most recent reports and 2026 candidates' reports with the Supervisor of Elections; 49 businesses both gave to a campaign and were paid in these records. Individual campaign donors are named only when they run a registered business; others are counted in totals. The simple version Who's in charge of what Elected boards set policy and budgets. The County Commission, each city commission or council, and the School Board vote on budgets, tax rates and big contracts. Appointed managers run operations. A county manager or city manager, hired by the board, runs departments and staff. Springfield and Parker have no manager; the board oversees staff directly and a city clerk handles administration. Five county officers are elected on their own. The Sheriff, Property Appraiser, Tax Collector, Clerk of Court and Supervisor of Elections each run their own office. The County Commission funds most of their budgets. Their pay is set by a state formula. Springfield · findings by year, oldest to newest: 7 → 11 → 8 FY2025 Clean opinion 8 findings Audit report Audit Adjusting Entries 2025-001 Repeat The auditors had to make significant corrections to the city's books. Management response: Will try to reduce adjustments; eliminating them would require hiring staff, which management calls cost prohibitive. Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards Preparation 2025-002 Repeat The city cannot prepare its own federal grant spending schedule; the auditors help, and multiple year-end grant entries were needed. Management response: Management considers auditor assistance cost-beneficial. Bank Reconciliations 2025-003 Repeat The pooled cash account in the ledger did not match the monthly and year-end bank reconciliations. Errors or fraud could go undetected. Management response: Dedicated employee plus management review of statements and a third-person review of entries now in place. Target Sep 30, 2026. Account Balances with Subsidiary Ledgers 2025-004 Repeat Receivables, customer deposits and payables did not agree with their detail ledgers and were not reconciled during the year. Management response: Training for finance staff and monthly management review of reconciliations. Target Sep 30, 2026. Month-end Closing 2025-005 Repeat The month-end checklist leaves out major balances, so monthly financial reports given to the Commission are not reliable. Management response: Will expand checklist, starting with bank reconciliations and payables. Target Sep 30, 2026. Activity Classification Review 2025-006 Repeat Many revenues and expenses were posted to the wrong accounts or netted together, hiding what was really collected and spent. Management response: Monthly financial statement review and staff training. Target Sep 30, 2026. Segregation of Duties 2025-007 Repeat Small staff means one person can approve, record and have custody of assets, including broad accounting system access. Management response: Will add mitigating controls; staff must be cross-trained as backups. Target Sep 30, 2026. Actual Expenditures Exceeded Budget in the General Fund 2025-008 General Fund spending exceeded the final adopted budget by about $8,069,872 without a budget amendment, violating s. 166.241(3) F.S. The auditor suggested budgeting for debt proceeds and similar sources (the year included the $15 million city complex loan). Management response: Will work to stay within budget and amend the budget as statute requires. Target Nov 30, 2026. Parker · findings by year, oldest to newest: 6 → 8 → 7 FY2025 Clean opinion 7 findings Audit report Significant Audit Adjustments 2025-001 Repeat The auditors had to propose adjustments before the city's books met accounting standards (GAAP). Material weakness. First reported in 2007. Management response: Hired a third-party accountant; expects fewer adjustments now that Hurricane Michael grant work is ending, but not elimination given limited staff. Target Sep 30, 2027. Lack of Segregation of Duties 2025-002 Repeat Too few staff to separate incompatible duties; material weakness reported since 2009. Management response: May never be fully resolved given staff size; management does not believe the cost of fixing it would provide substantial benefit. Target Sep 30, 2027. Reporting Requirements for Grants 2025-003 Repeat The audit was not finished within 9 months of year end, so the federal Single Audit package was not filed on time with the Federal Audit Clearinghouse. The city could lose grant funding. Management response: Staff turnover delayed reporting; city expects to correct in the coming year. Insufficient Documentation Supporting Law Enforcement Trust Fund Revenue 2025-004 The city booked $36,652 from disposed criminal-case evidence as Law Enforcement Trust Fund revenue but could not show a forfeiture judgment or court order proving the money legally belonged to the city. Revenue and fund balance may be overstated by $36,652. Management response: See city's corrective action plan in report. Failure to Timely Transfer Tax Increment Revenues to CRA Trust Fund 2025-005 Repeat State law (s. 163.387 F.S.) requires each taxing authority to pay its tax increment to the CRA by January 1. The county paid 4 days late and the city did not pay its own share before year end, leaving the CRA trust fund short about $122,929. Management response: Procedures established; the city TIF payment will be built into the budget so it is transferred by January 1. Target Sep 30, 2027. OPEB Census Errors 2025-006 Repeat Employee data sent to the actuary for the retiree-health (OPEB) valuation had multiple errors, producing an inaccurate valuation and delaying the audit. Management response: Errors stem from the prior valuation; a new valuation with corrected data and a more detailed census review will be done in FY2026. Target Sep 30, 2027. Retirement Expense Not Reviewed Timely and Rates Not Updated 2025-007 The city did not update new state FRS contribution rates effective July 1, 2025 in its payroll system for months, understating retirement expense and liability by about $20,000. Management response: Rates updated in FY2026; actual contributions remitted through the state portal were correct; monthly reconciliation and rate-change review will be added. Target Sep 30, 2027. FY2024 Clean opinion 8 findings Audit report Significant Audit Adjustments 2024-001 Repeat Auditor-proposed adjustments needed to meet GAAP. Management response: Not corrected; lack of resources. Lack of Segregation of Duties 2024-002 Repeat Too few staff to separate duties. Management response: Not corrected; lack of resources. Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards 2024-003 Repeat Weak controls over preparing the financial statements and the federal awards schedule (material weakness); repeat of 2023-003 and 2022-003. Management response: Reported corrected in FY2025. Failure to Timely Transfer Tax Increment Revenues to CRA Trust Fund - City Allocation 2024-004 For the current year and the two years before, the city did not calculate and transfer its required share of tax increment to its CRA. Management response: Partially corrected in FY2025 (past amounts paid but not on time). Reporting Requirements for Grants 2024-005 Repeat Single Audit package not filed on time with the Federal Audit Clearinghouse. Management response: Not corrected; staff turnover. OPEB Census Errors 2024-006 Inaccurate employee data given to the OPEB actuary. Management response: New valuation planned for FY2026. Lack of Review and Reconciliation of Certain Account Activity 2024-007 Certain account activity was not consistently reviewed and reconciled. Management response: Reported corrected in FY2025. Reimbursement Requests Not Formally Approved Before Submission (federal, AL 97.036 FEMA Public Assistance) 2024-101 Hurricane Michael FEMA reimbursement requests were submitted without documented city approval. Significant deficiency in internal control over compliance; no questioned costs. Management response: Reported corrected in FY2025. Management response: Not expected to be corrected soon due to lack of resources. Lack of Segregation of Duties 2023-002 Repeat Too few staff to separate duties. Management response: Same as above. Management response: See report. State auditor reports Florida Auditor General reviews beyond the yearly audit. Operational Audit (period Oct. 2022 - Jan. 2024) (Report No. 2025-095, January 2025) Finding 1. Heavy turnover: from Jan. 2020 to Aug. 2024 the City Administrator position turned over 3 times, City Clerk 2 times, and City Accountant 3 times (vacant 495 days). Records showed allegations of a negative workplace and conflicts between management and elected officials. Finding 2. Audits and annual financial reports were filed late for FY2020-21 through FY2022-23 (FY2021-22 audit was 362 days late). The Department of Revenue withheld $37,137 ($29,166 half-cent sales tax + $7,971 municipal revenue sharing) as of August 2024. Finding 3. Competitive procurement not followed: 5 purchases totaling $564,092 (including $250,000 disaster debris removal, $130,772 fuel from the same local vendor for at least 19 years, $110,260 yard waste) were not competitively selected; other bids/RFPs lacked advertising documentation. Finding 4. 9 purchases totaling $1 million lacked City Council approval required for purchases over $10,000; purchase orders were not used as required, and receipt of goods/services was not always documented. Finding 5. The city paid a contractor the same $450,031 invoice twice; the contractor refunded $328,964 on Dec. 13, 2023 (the duplicate less $121,067 retainage). Finding 6. The city kept paying its contracted City Accountant after the agreement expired (April 2021) and issued 1099s instead of W-2s without documenting why she was treated as an independent contractor. Finding 7. Application security: user access privileges were not limited to what was necessary. Finding 8. IT access was not always promptly removed when no longer needed. Finding 9. No policies for reporting, investigating and communicating known or suspected fraud.
